summary: Comparing decimals is a place-value skill, not digit-counting. You compare from the highest place: any whole-number part first, then tenths, then hundredths, then thousandths, until the digits differ, reasoning aloud ('0.38 is 3 tenths and 8 hundredths, which is less than 4 tenths'). The core difficulty is false analogy with whole numbers, producing two opposite faulty rules: 'longer-is-larger' (claiming 0.45 > 0.5 'because 45 > 5', treating the tail as a whole number) and 'shorter-is-larger' (claiming 0.4 > 0.87, from reading 0.4 as 1/4 vs 0.87 as 1/87, or from over-applying 'tenths are bigger than hundredths'). Both faulty rules give correct answers on tidy same-length pairs, so RAGGED decimals (different numbers of places) are essential to expose them. Teach through place-value reasoning and a length model, and establish that annexing zeros (0.7 = 0.70 = 0.700) does not change value.
misconceptions: Longer-is-larger: judging the decimal with more digits as larger (0.45 > 0.5, 0.311 > 0.4), treating the tail as a whole number.
Shorter-is-larger (fraction-thinking): 0.4 > 0.87 because 0.4 is read as 1/4 and 0.87 as 1/87 ('sharing among fewer gives more').
Shorter-is-larger (tenths>hundredths): 0.4 > 0.87 from the over-applied partial truth that a tenth is bigger than a hundredth.
Believing annexing a zero changes value (0.7 ≠ 0.70).
Comparing digit-by-digit from the right, or comparing the fractional parts as isolated whole numbers regardless of place.

activities.title: Order ragged decimals against a length model
steps: Before using any model, predict the order of ragged decimals from smallest to largest and say why, e.g. for 0.4, 0.38, 0.312, 0.5.
Represent each decimal as a bar or length drawn to a common scale (for example a Linear Arithmetic Block / bar model), then check your predicted order against the lengths.

State the correct order (0.312 < 0.38 < 0.4 < 0.5) and justify it in place-value language: 0.312 and 0.38 both have 3 tenths, so they are smaller than 0.4 (4 tenths) and 0.5 (5 tenths); among the 3-tenths numbers, 0.312 (3 tenths 1 hundredth) is less than 0.38 (3 tenths 8 hundredths).

Also compare the counterexample ragged pairs 0.4 vs 0.87, 0.9 vs 0.11, and 0.45 vs 0.405: predict first, then check each against the length model and in place-value words. These pairs deliberately trip both faulty rules — for example 0.45 vs 0.405 tempts longer-is-larger (405 looks bigger than 45), yet 0.45 (4 tenths 5 hundredths) is larger than 0.405 (4 tenths 0 hundredths 5 thousandths); and on the 0.4/0.38/0.312/0.5 set a shorter-is-larger learner can still land the right order.
Locate the decimals on a number line and, where helpful, zoom between 0.3 and 0.4 to see 0.38 and 0.312 separated in the hundredths.
Compare 0.7 with 0.70 (optionally using an annex-zero toggle or shading) and explain why trailing zeros do not change the value.
activities.insight: The decimal with more digits is not automatically larger, and the one with fewer digits is not automatically larger either; size is decided by the highest place where the digits differ. A length/number-line model shows that more digits need not mean more length (0.38 is shorter than 0.4, but 0.87 is longer than 0.4). Annexing trailing zeros gives decimals the same number of decimal places without changing their value.

activities.title: Name and resist the whole-number rule (correct vs incorrect cards)
steps: Look at side-by-side comparison cards, one clearly labelled correct and one clearly labelled wrong, e.g. '0.45 > 0.5' (labelled wrong) beside '0.45 < 0.5' (labelled correct).
Say out loud which faulty rule produced the wrong card ('longer-is-larger: it counted 45 against 5') and explain why it fails here.
Write or state the place-value reason the correct card holds (0.5 is 5 tenths; 0.45 is 4 tenths 5 hundredths; 5 tenths is more).
Before answering each new pair, flag the rule you must NOT use, then compare correctly.
activities.insight: The error is partly a failure to inhibit the whole-number rule, not only missing knowledge; naming the misconception and inspecting clearly-labelled correct/incorrect examples side by side helps a learner catch and override it.

activities.title: Show equivalence and area with hundredths grids
steps: Shade 0.4 and 0.38 each on a 10×10 hundredths grid and compare the shaded areas.
Shade 0.7 on one grid and 0.70 on another, and explain why seven tenths fills the same area as seventy hundredths.
Use an aligned place-value chart (points lined up) to read each decimal digit by digit, starting from tenths, and state which decimal is larger and why.
activities.insight: Decimals can be compared by area as well as by length, and both representations show that annexing a zero (0.7 = 0.70) preserves value while more digits need not mean more size. (Note: the source synthesis treats length as the clearest magnitude model for this topic; the grid is a complementary reference.)

checkQuestion: Put these in order from smallest to largest and show me how you decided: 0.4, 0.38, 0.312, 0.5. Then tell me — is 0.7 the same size as 0.70, and how do you know?
checkAnswer: 0.312 < 0.38 < 0.4 < 0.5. Reasoning by place value: 0.312 and 0.38 have 3 tenths (smaller), and 0.312 (3 tenths 1 hundredth) is less than 0.38 (3 tenths 8 hundredths); 0.4 and 0.5 have 4 and 5 tenths. 0.7 = 0.70 — seven tenths equals seventy hundredths; the trailing zero does not change the value.
